findings: excludeDeleted() hardcodes the column name 'deleted_at' and is applied uniformly to every table by the shared search() function, but the users table has no deleted_at column at all — it uses is_deleted instead — so the filter's column assumption doesn't match the real per-table schema.

Because unknownColumnMode is 'silent-skip', the query builder silently drops the deleted_at clause when it runs against users instead of raising an error, so no soft-delete filter is applied to user search at all — this is the direct mechanism causing deleted accounts to leak into results while orders (which does have deleted_at) is correctly filtered.

The silent-skip mode was deliberately configured 'to avoid 500s' on optional filters, which trades correctness for availability and fails open (a missing filter silently means 'include everything') rather than failing closed (excluding everything) — the wrong default for a visibility/exclusion filter.

This is a systemic risk, not a one-off: since the same excludeDeleted()/search() functions are explicitly shared across all search endpoints, any other table whose column names don't match what the shared filter logic assumes will silently and invisibly lose that filter too, with no error to signal it.

The two tables implement incompatible soft-delete conventions with no shared contract enforced: orders.deleted_at is a nullable TIMESTAMP capturing deletion time, while users.is_deleted is a NOT NULL BOOLEAN with no timestamp — there is no single soft-delete interface that both tables actually conform to, which is what let the generic function's assumption go unnoticed.

The resulting defect is a real access/visibility leak, not cosmetic: deleted user accounts (and their data) are discoverable through generic search in production, confirmed by support, meaning records that should be hidden are exposed.
